A Raisin in the Sun. Lorraine Hansberry's 1959 play follows the African American Younger family in Chicago as they await a life insurance check following their patriarch's death. The windfall becomes a source of hope and conflict as family members pursue competing dreams—education, business, dignity—against the backdrop of segregation and limited opportunity.

This was the first major Broadway play written by a Black woman and featuring an all-Black cast. It won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award and made Hansberry the youngest winner at the time. The title comes from Langston Hughes' poem Harlem: "What happens to a dream deferred? Does it dry up like a raisin in the sun?"

The father's dream was to own a business. His widow Lena wants to buy a house in a white neighborhood. His son Walter wants to invest in a liquor store. The family's neighbor George Murchison, a wealthy educated Black man, rejects his African heritage and embraces assimilationist values—a counterpoint to Walter's hunger for wealth. The family's move to an all-white neighborhood becomes both a personal victory and an act of resistance against housing discrimination. Each family member must reconcile their individual aspirations with collective survival and dignity.

Lorraine Hansberry created her landmark work asserting Black identity and family resilience in American drama. The play's historical significance lies in expanding representation and authorship on American stages. The Crucible examines moral integrity under social pressure and threats to family. Death of a Salesman is a contemporary family tragedy, though A Raisin in the Sun adds the dimension of racial oppression to economic despair. And Our Town offers an earlier vision of American community life, while A Raisin in the Sun challenges whose America that vision includes.
